source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning
finding: Defines the three-phase cycle. Wake: solve tasks by search guided by a neural recognition model. Sleep-abstraction: refactor solved programs and grow the library. Sleep-dreaming: train the recognition model on replays of solved tasks and on fantasies sampled from the library.
numbers: Cycle run for 8 to 20 iterations per domain; six main domains plus physics and recursion.
limits: Search cost is large; typical convergence about a day on 20-100 CPUs.
agent_relevance: Direct template for a wake/abstract/dream cycle over a subgoal library.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: text editing result
finding: Trained on 128 generated text tasks, tested on 108 SyGuS 2017 problems. Learning raised solve rate from 3.7% to 79.6% and cut mean search time from 235 s to 40 s.
numbers: 10 min limit: 3.7% -> 79.6%. CVC4 (best competition solver, 1 h, 8 CPUs) 82.4%; DreamCoder with that budget 84.3%.
limits: One benchmark; SyGuS 2017 chosen because later sets are at ceiling for custom solvers.
agent_relevance: Shows a learned library plus a learned guide can cut search cost about 6x while keeping coverage.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: list processing
finding: 218 list tasks, 50/50 train/test, 15 examples each. About 20 new routines learned; it rediscovered filter, then max, then nth largest, then sort, each built on the last.
numbers: 218 tasks; about 20 learned library routines.
limits: Tasks taken from earlier work; small domain.
agent_relevance: Library growth is hierarchical: later abstractions reuse earlier ones. Our subgoal library should allow nesting.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: ablations and baselines
finding: Across six domains the full model solved the most held-out tasks. In LOGO graphics and tower building no alternative solved more than 60% of held-out tasks while DreamCoder reached nearly 100%. Memorize baselines (store whole solutions, no compression) did worse.
numbers: Library depth correlates with tasks solved r = 0.79. Enumeration baseline: 24 h per task, up to 400 million programs. Mean solve time 54.1 s, median 15.0 s. Error bars: 5 runs.
quote: no alternative model ever solves more than 60% of held-out tasks
limits: Per-arm bar values were not read from the figure.
agent_relevance: Compression, not hoarding, is what helps: storing raw solutions is not enough.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: dreams and recognition model
finding: Early dreams are simple and unstructured. After 20 cycles dreams recombine learned concepts in ways never seen in wake. Recognition-network task similarity aligns with the code used in solutions (p < 1e-4, chi-square, pre vs post).
numbers: LOGO set 160 images; tower set 107 tasks; both 50/50 split; 20 cycles.
limits: Dream figures show the most interesting dreams across five runs; random samples only in the supplement.
agent_relevance: Fantasy data only helps once the library is rich. Early dreaming from a poor library adds little.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: physics laws and recursion from near scratch
finding: From generic map/fold/arithmetic it learned 93% of 60 physics laws in 8 cycles (vector algebra first, then inverse-square schema). From 1959 Lisp primitives it rediscovered fold/unfold, solving all 20 tasks after about five days on 64 CPUs.
numbers: 93% of 60 laws after 8 cycles; 20/20 recursion tasks; about one CPU-year for the origami basis.
limits: Authors themselves say learning from so little is unlikely to be the best route.
agent_relevance: Cost warning: from-scratch library growth is very expensive; start from a good base set of operators.

source: Hinton, Dayan, Frey, Neal (1995) The wake-sleep algorithm for unsupervised neural networks
finding: Original wake-sleep: a generative network and a recognition network train each other. Wake: recognition samples latents for real data, generative weights learn. Sleep: generative network dreams, recognition weights learn to invert the dream.
numbers: Not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Sleep phase minimises KL in the wrong direction (stated in Bornschein & Bengio); not a bound on likelihood.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal root of 'train the search net on dreams'.

source: Bornschein & Bengio (2015) Reweighted wake-sleep (ICLR)
finding: Reinterprets wake-sleep as importance sampling with the inference net as proposal. Original wake-sleep equals K=1 sample; more samples give a less biased gradient. A stronger q layer (NADE) beats sigmoid belief nets.
numbers: K=5 samples in training, K=100,000 for test estimate. MNIST three-layer SBN: sleep-only q update about -93.4 nats, wake-only about -92.8 (table text garbled; check before quoting).
limits: Gradient is still biased in log space.
agent_relevance: A single dream sample gives a biased signal; draw several candidates and weight them in code.

source: Dayan, Hinton, Neal, Zemel (1995) The Helmholtz machine
finding: Frames perception as inference in a generative model learned with a recognition model. Basis for wake-sleep.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Claim from memory of the abstract only.
agent_relevance: Conceptual root: the guide net amortises inference over the library's generative model.

source: Bowers et al. (2023) Top-down synthesis for library learning (Stitch), POPL
finding: Replaces DreamCoder's rewrite-based sleep-abstraction with top-down corpus-guided search. Much faster and lighter at the same or better compression.
numbers: 3-4 orders of magnitude faster, 2 orders less memory than DreamCoder. Compression ratios 2.55x to 11.57x in 0.19-60.16 s on its domains. Held-out test: random 80/20 splits repeated 50 times. Early stopping with under 2% of compute recovers most gain.
limits: Quality measured by compression, not downstream solve rate.
agent_relevance: The abstraction step can be cheap and anytime, which fits a token budget.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code (ICLR)
finding: Replaces enumerative wake search with an LLM, keeps Stitch for abstraction, adds AutoDoc (LLM names and documents each abstraction). Online test solve rate, mean of 3 runs: REGEX DreamCoder 43.93, LLM Solver 76.13, LILO 77.07; CLEVR 94.50, 88.67, 96.76; LOGO 28.53, 32.13, 48.95.
numbers: LILO max: REGEX 93.20, CLEVR 99.03, LOGO 73.87. Std of LILO on LOGO 9.46; LLM Solver on REGEX 12.04.
limits: Large run variance; REGEX gain over LLM Solver (+0.9) is inside noise. Codex used for solving, gpt-3.5/gpt-4 for AutoDoc.
agent_relevance: LLM wake plus symbolic compression works, but gains are domain-dependent.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Stitch alone hurt the LLM; AutoDoc repaired it
finding: Giving the LLM unnamed Stitch abstractions lowered solve rate versus plain LLM. Adding AutoDoc names recovered +9.73 points (REGEX) and +2.27 (CLEVR); no gain on LOGO.
numbers: Change from compression alone vs LLM Solver: -30.60 REGEX, -2.91 CLEVR, -11.11 LOGO. AutoDoc effect: +9.73, +2.27, +0.00. One LLM synthesis round is estimated equal to 48 CPU-hours of DreamCoder search.
limits: Cost comparison is the authors' estimate.
agent_relevance: A new library entry must carry a name and a usage note, or the model cannot use it. Store entries as readable text.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: online versus offline protocol
finding: Offline test hands each learned library to a fixed enumerative search with a fixed time budget, isolating library quality from solver strength.
numbers: Offline table is partly garbled in extracted text; per-arm numbers not recorded here.
limits: Protocol finding only; read the PDF table before quoting offline scores.
agent_relevance: Evaluate a library with a fixed solver to separate library quality from solver strength.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with LLMs
finding: Skill library of executable code, grown by the LLM when a task is verified done; no gradient. Versus AutoGPT, ReAct and Reflexion over 160 iterations.
numbers: 63 unique items (3.3x), 2.3x longer distances; tech-tree milestones faster: wood 15.3x, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x; only agent to reach diamond. Ablation: random curriculum -93% items; no self-verification -73%; GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4 gives 5.7x fewer.
quote: VOYAGER w/o skill library exhibits a tendency to plateau in the later stages.
limits: Single environment; gains blend curriculum, library and verification. Removing the library only caused a late plateau.
agent_relevance: Skill library here is wake-only: no abstraction or dream phase. Self-verification gate matches our code checks.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions (ICML)
finding: Gradient-free sleep-abstraction by LLM: refactor, verify by execution that output is unchanged, keep helper functions. CodeLlama-13B gains: LOGO +11.5, Date +26.1, TextCraft +8.1 points.
numbers: CodeLlama-13B LOGO 45.6 -> 57.1, outperforming GPT-3.5 without abstractions by 19.2 points. TextCraft CodeLlama-34B 22.2 -> 30.8. Learned from about 200 examples.
limits: On MATH and TabMWP gains were smaller; Lemur-70B gave many empty outputs and results were within error.
agent_relevance: Execution-verified refactoring is a safe abstraction rule: keep a new subgoal only if old results still reproduce.

source: Stengel-Eskin et al. (2024) ReGAL ablations
finding: Removing parts of the loop hurts: retry of failed refactors, curriculum ordering short-to-long, pruning and editing the code bank all matter.
numbers: Dev, CodeLlama-13B. Full: LOGO 55.0, Date 77.0, TextCraft 34.12. No retry 48.3/51.9/30.43. No curriculum 36.3/56.6/28.78. No prune 52.0/65.5/25.26. No edit 53.3/69.6/27.35.
limits: Dev splits, one model.
agent_relevance: Order easy to hard when folding solutions into the library, and prune.

source: Wang et al. (2024) TroVE: inducing verifiable and efficient toolboxes
finding: Training-free toolbox that grows by using, adding and periodically trimming functions. Claims higher accuracy with 79-98% smaller toolboxes on 11 datasets; human verification 31% faster and 13% more accurate.
numbers: Toolboxes 79-98% smaller; 31% faster, 13% more accurate human checking.
limits: Reuse as the cause of the gain is questioned by the next line. Only skimmed (abstract and intro) this session.
agent_relevance: Trimming is part of consolidation: small libraries are easier to check.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: Audit of LEGO-Prover and TroVE. Learned functions are almost never reused; gains come from self-correction and self-consistency, not library reuse.
numbers: LEGO-Prover logs: 1,233 lemmas (6%) reached the prover; exactly one lemma reused once, none twice. TroVE: 15 learned functions, 3 successful reuses in 3,201 MATH test questions. Zero-reuse ablation solved only 1 problem fewer (miniF2F validation, 50 attempts, 2 trials).
quote: function reuse is extremely infrequent on miniF2F and MATH
limits: Math only; DreamCoder-style domains (graphics, strings) not tested. Indirect reuse not fully ruled out.
agent_relevance: Do not credit the library without an ablation that blocks reuse. Count reuse in our own logs.

source: Berlot-Attwell et al. (2024) TroVE ablation detail
finding: Disabling TroVE's IMPORT mode (no library use) kept or beat baseline accuracy on several MATH splits.
numbers: Example columns: intermediate algebra 0.120 +/- 0.006 vs 0.134 +/- 0.014 (ablation); number 0.258 vs 0.290; geometry 0.058 vs 0.050. CodeLlama-7B-Instruct. Which row is baseline vs ablation was read from garbled table text.
limits: Small gaps; significance on two splits per authors.
agent_relevance: Many sampled attempts can mimic a library gain. Keep G4 in mind.

source: Mnih et al. (2013) Playing Atari with deep reinforcement learning
finding: Experience replay in deep RL: store transitions in replay memory D and update on random minibatches to break correlation. Beat prior methods on 6 of 7 games and a human expert on 3.
numbers: Seven Atari games; outperformed prior on six; above expert human on three.
limits: Uniform sampling; later work shows non-uniform replay helps.
agent_relevance: Origin of replay as decorrelating and re-using rare experience.

source: Schaul et al. (2016) Prioritized experience replay (ICLR)
finding: Replay transitions in proportion to TD error. Beats uniform replay on 41 of 49 Atari games; learning about twice as fast.
numbers: DQN median normalised score 48% -> 106%. Double DQN median (57 games) 111% -> 128%, mean 418% -> 551%. Games above human, DQN 49 games: 15 -> 25.
limits: Mean dominated by Video Pinball; rank-based and proportional variants win on different games.
agent_relevance: Which stored item to replay matters: prioritise by surprise or failure, not at random.

source: Shin, Lee, Kim, Kim (2017) Continual learning with deep generative replay
finding: A generator (scholar) replays pseudo-data of old tasks so the solver does not forget. A solver trained alone sequentially suffers catastrophic forgetting. Random Gaussian noise paired with recorded responses did not help.
numbers: MNIST: solvers trained from replay stayed near 98.5-98.8% on full test data across five sequential solvers.
limits: Image tasks; small scale; replay only as good as the generator.
agent_relevance: Generated replays must resemble real tasks; noise is useless.

source: Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks
finding: Elastic weight consolidation protects weights important to old tasks as an alternative to replay.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Main non-replay rival.
agent_relevance: A text library has no weights to forget; forgetting there means pruning and retrieval failure.

source: McClelland, McNaughton, O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems
finding: Fast hippocampal learning with slow interleaved replay into neocortex avoids catastrophic interference.
numbers: Not opened. Covered by subfield 08 of this series.
limits: See 08_complementary_learning_systems; not repeated.
agent_relevance: Replay should be interleaved with old items, not only recent ones.

source: Ellis et al. (2018) Learning libraries of subroutines for neurally-guided Bayesian program induction
finding: Predecessor of DreamCoder: library learning plus neural guidance.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Superseded by DreamCoder.
agent_relevance: Backward citation.

source: Synthesis across LILO, ReGAL, Voyager, TroVE and the single-use audit
finding: In 2023-24 LLM library learners, gains are real on domain-structured tasks (graphics, text games, Minecraft) and doubtful on open math. None of the LLM systems read here trains on fantasies: the LLM replaces the neural guide, so the dreaming phase has no LLM test.
numbers: Examples: ReGAL LOGO +11.5; LILO LOGO 28.53 -> 48.95; Voyager 3.3x items; TroVE reuse 3 of 3,201.
limits: Cross-paper comparison of different models and metrics.
agent_relevance: For our agent: keep wake plus verified abstraction; test dreaming only as an ablation.
